utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, and Your Honour, Judge Hall. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Matthew Gillett, Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May the record reflect that we sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis; Judge Mindua being absent. Mr. Zivanovic, is your next witness ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. First of all, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Borivoje Milinkovic. 29 January 1955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read a solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you that the solemn declarations that you are about to make does expose you to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or false evidence to this Tribunal. Can I now ask you to read the solemn declaration the court usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milinkovic, although we know each other, I will introduce myself for the record. I am Zoran Zivanovic, and I represent Goran Hadzic here. First of all, I should like to ask you, if you remember, that on the 9th and 10th June in 2003 you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor; that is to say, the OTP investigators of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D2328.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will on the screen presently and you will be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we have a tab number, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, sorry. It is tab 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, you will see the English translation of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we could scroll down a little, the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see your signature here?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move on to page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On this page, can you see your signature?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think you've seen this statement and your signatures are on every page of this statement, but I wouldn't like to go through all of it. Along with this statement, you also identified certain photographs that were shown to you by OTP investigators on that occasion. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will only show you a couple of those. It's 1D2328.1. The next tab, tab 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have to see again all these photographs. In any case, you recall they were shown to you and you recognised some of the people, and this is a list of those you identified. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During our proofing session and while we were reviewing again this statement, you made some corrections to the statement you've just seen in Serbian. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see you don't have the statement before you.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I left it behind. I was told that I couldn't take it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I have a B/C/S copy here that I could provide to the witness, if Your Honour -- with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see on the screen 1D2328, please. And we can move to the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, what -- what's the tab number from the next document you're asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 1D2328 is the statement of Mr. -- of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. It's -- tab -- tab 31, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 31, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is said to be confidential on your list. On your exhibit list it is said to be confidential. Little bit surprising, but I will check.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's correct. It should not be -- it should not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- broadcast, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't understand that any protective measures have been applied for this witness and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: -- so we don't understand why his statement would be confidential and not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree that -- I think it was an error that this particular statement was put as a confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: An error on your list, you mean or whatever other --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I was a little bit confused as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we do agree there is no reason to have it confidential. Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- then we can broadcast it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at paragraph 4 of your statement. I believe you wanted to make some corrections considering the schools you finished. Would you tell us what those corrections are.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a lower music school, not higher music school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, in the last sentence it says that up to 1990 you had been living for five years in Dalj. You want to correct something?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I always lived in Dalj except that I travelled very often for my work and I would be away for five or six months at a time, and this text reads as if I had lived only for five years in Dalj by 1990. I lived in Dalj all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 6. In the second sentence it says you joined the SDS because the programme of the party, which was democratic and nationalist but not chauvinistic. What did you want to correct here?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to have it described as national, not nationalist. Because nationalist has a connotation of chauvinistic. It's bordering on chauvinistic. What I meant to say was national programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe briefly your understanding of the difference between "national" and "nationalist."

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It's the same as if you say a Serbian person and a great Serb. It kind of borders on chauvinistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 19, which is on the next page, paragraph 11, you can see it in front of you. It refers to a baptism ceremony. What did you mean to say? What kind of baptism ceremony?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It says at this meeting of the SDS [as interpreted] we organised the baptism for the Serbian singing society, Lira, Lira.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Serbian singing society, Lira, L-i-r-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe there's another mistake here. Did you say it was a meeting of the SDS or another party?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a meeting of the HDZ, Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems that ... Your Honours, I noted one error in the transcript in line 8. When I asked after my question could you just repeat the name, the answer was -- it was the Serbian singing society of the Lira. It was not my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after that is my question. I believe that there is another mistake here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that would be a new -- a new question; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 21, which is on the next page, you said, among other things, that to this day you are still not sure what the aims of the Serbian Autonomous District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem were because at the beginning there were no clear objectives. What did you mean to correct here?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: There's some confusion here. What I meant is that objectives existed. One objective was cultural autonomy, but it has to do with the Serbian Krajina when the SBS -- when the SBWS loses its purpose, its meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there some objectives related to the outcome of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After we got the results of the referendum, we just continued pursuing the same policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was decided at the referendum? What was the question?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the referendum: That Serbs were a constituent people and they want cultural autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall a referendum as to whether the Serbs want to remain within Yugoslavia or be annexed to some other country?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. We always wanted to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, and this could wait for -- for cross-examination to clarify. But just before we move on to the next paragraph, the witness said at line 4 of page 8: "One objective was cultural autonomy but it has to do with the Serbian Krajina when the SBS -- when the SBWS loses its purpose, its meaning." And I'm just wondering if we could clarify the time-frame that we're talking about here in relation to the comments on this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the previous paragraph, number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said what is stated in this paragraph -- first of all, did you say it in these terms?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Possibly. But I kind of trail off sometimes and the interpreters must have a hard time. Can I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a later period of the Republic of Serbian Krajina because it was proclaimed at a later stage. So quite naturally, the Serbian District does not have the same status in terms of its president and its government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to this later. It's enough for now. Please look at paragraph 23. It says that the election of Goran Hadzic as president was a sign that he had some connections and contacts in Serbia. When you talk about the election of Goran Hadzic as president, did you mean president of the government; that is to say, prime minister of the SBWS, or the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, or both?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not both. I meant president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 it says that while you were living in Dalj, one day you were taken to the police station. You wanted to specify which police station.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the police station of Osijek, 25 kilometres from Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 28, about the action to take Dalj. I believe that you wanted to say something about the date, about the time when you arrived from Serbia in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did not arrive on the 1st of August but on the 31st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that you also wanted to say something about the date in paragraph 29. Again, this date has to do with the action in Dalj.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Instead of the 2nd of August, it should read the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, paragraph 29, it says that on that day you returned to Dalj. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that while I was talking, this is how it was translated or interpreted. I had left almost a month before that, and that's why I thought it would be a good thing that -- to say that I returned. In any case, on that day I entered Dalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And let's link that to the previous paragraph. You're actually describing one and the same event in paragraphs 28 and 29, if I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the dates are different. The first date is the 31st of July, and the second date is the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 33, which is on the following page, you describe the transport of corpses which took place after the fighting around Dalj. You wanted to tell us how that transport was organised. Can you do that now?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: The military negotiated the transport of corpses from Dalj. Cooler trucks arrived from Osijek together with ambulances, and they transported some of the corpses, whereas some still remained in Dalj. The corpses that remained there were there throughout the afternoon. We buried those people in the Catholic cemetery because they were all Catholics, Croats. That's the only thing that we could do for these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the military negotiated the transport of corpses, who did they negotiate with?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. But everything was under the military command, and none of the locals could talk to the other side, to the people from Osijek. The only body that could do that was the military. I don't know who they negotiated with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question may have been a bit ambiguous. I didn't mean the person. I meant the party. Did they negotiate with a civilian body in Dalj or with a body from outside of the territory?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: In Dalj, you couldn't talk to the civilian authorities because there were none. The local community had stopped existing. There was only the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned cooler trucks and ambulances that had arrived from Osijek. Who controlled Osijek at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian side controlled Osijek. Although Yugoslavia still existed at the time, we thought that Osijek was controlled by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at paragraph 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 35, it says: "During my term in the government, there was no general policy in the government of the SAO SBWS on the presence of non-Serbs in the area. I think that the policy was for everyone to remain where they were. As for Goran Hadzic, I don't know whether he had an opinion on this issue." Could you please specify?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: During my term in the government, we didn't discuss the policy of resettlement, expulsion, or the departure of Croats from their places of residence. Besides, many were from mixed marriages so it would have not made much sense for anybody to move out or to be expelled. And as for Mr. Goran Hadzic, I don't know if he had a different opinion. Even if he did, I never heard him talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government have a specific policy towards the Serbs who resided there as opposed to the non-Serbs who resided there? How did the government treat all the citizens who lived in the area?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: The government did not make a distinction. Nobody was asked to declare themselves either as a -- Serbs, Croats, or Hungarians. They were all equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government pursue different policies towards the Serbs as opposed to the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, the government did not deal with that issue at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 44, you were shown a document dated 5 October 1991. Milorad Stricevic signed it as the chief of security? You said that you had never heard of that incident which is mentioned in the document. How did Milorad Stricevic introduce himself in Dalj? As the chief of security or differently?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: From the very outset, he introduced him as a colonel. All of us locals didn't know whether he was really a colonel or not. To this very day, I don't know. I know for a fact that he was not a member of the military because he did some other things. I know -- I knew him from before the war. I don't know how he happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 47, you talk about a meeting in Vukovar when members of the government met at Velepromet. First of all, when you say that you were delayed by about two to three minutes, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: May I? Last time when I testified I thought it was two to three minutes, but it must have been 10 to 15 minutes. I had to go to the church, I had to load some books and other things into my car, so it must have been 10 to 15 minutes, not two to three minutes. That would have been too short.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first sentence in paragraph 47, you say that it was not a government session. What was it? What took place at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that it was not a government session. If it had been a government session, I would have received an invitation to the government session. It was just a meeting. I did not even know that it would be at Velepromet. I thought would take place anywhere in the -- in liberated Vukovar. There would have been an agenda. There was none. No minutes were taken. The meeting -- minutes of the previous session were not adopted. It did not look like a government session. It did not have the form of a government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 48, it says, inter alia, that you didn't know what military was there. What did you mean when you said that you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was misinterpreted. I meant unit. It could have been the Novi Sad Corps or the guards unit, and then you would have known who the commander was. When I read this, it seems that I didn't even know what army was there, which is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you say that at that meeting nobody mentioned Ovcara or the establishment of prison or a detention facility for temporary accommodation of prisoners and that you heard that for the first time during the interview. Did you mean the interview with the investigators?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also say in this paragraph that there were talks about the construction of a prison in Beli Manastir, that you were aware of that. Let's be more precise. Was that discussed at the meeting at Velepromet or elsewhere, at some other meetings of the government beforehand or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: That was discussed at other meetings of the government. On that day, nobody mentioned the construction of a prison in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at paragraph -- paragraphs 56 and 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, do you remember this part where you say that various statements were read to you after they had been given by members of the JNA. And I'm talking about that interview.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? That was a long time ago, so I don't remember. It was quite a number of years ago. I don't know what was read to me at the time. I can't stand by this. I'm under oath. I can't confirm what it says here because I'm not sure that it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you to look at paragraph 56. Does that also apply to the following paragraph where some statements are mentioned as well, also given by JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraphs 56 and 57 are closely linked. I simply can't remember that anything was read out to me. I really can't stand by these two paragraphs because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 60, you were asked about the -- the destruction of the -- Orthodox and Catholic churches in Tovarnik or, rather, the damages they sustained. In the last sentence, you mentioned a third side which may have been to blame for the damages to the Catholic church. What did you have in mind when you mentioned a third side?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean -- I meant atheists; non-believers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 65. You meant to say here or, rather, you -- you wanted to say about Hadzic's visits to Milosevic. Do you remember the periods when that happened?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that was when pressures were put to bear on to adopt the Vance-Owen Plan. That may have been some time after new year, and the year I have in mind is the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since it says here, if you read it you will find it, that during the time you were a minister in the government of the SAO SBWS, Goran Hadzic often said that he had travelled to Belgrade and visited Slobodan Milosevic. Does that mean that those visits to Slobodan Milosevic happened during that period when peacekeeping forces arrived and when the Vance-Owen Plan was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the period I had in mind. Although I became minister before that, that's the period I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at paragraph 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you wanted to make a correction there. You said it was your belief that Goran Hadzic was under somebody's influence. What did you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: He looked very scared to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 71 of your statement, you noticed that one word you used to refer to the church official who was in Dalj was not adequately phrased. What was that word?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Orthodox "vladika."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph is that? In the translation, the word is bishop, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: "Vladika" is not bishop. Bishop is a Catholic term. I'm not saying that bishop is an ugly word, but we just should make the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said you would like to clarify one more thing here. It says that Arkan and his men were accommodated near the school. First of all, which was place were we talking about? Which town?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was talking about Dalj. Arkan and his men were based Erdut, but two or three of his men guarded the residence of the patriarch where "vladika" was staying and that is close to the school. That's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To get a better understanding of this, what is "vladika"?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: "Vladika" is the highest rank, like in the army. Below him are lower-ranking priests. He lives like a monk. He's totally devoted to the church. He doesn't get married. He's devoted to the church and the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your understanding, was there any need for Arkan's Men to guard the vladika? Was he threatened in any way so as to need security?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what bothered me. He was not threatened. There was nobody to threatened him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Objection. There was a leading question there. I understand these are corrections to the statement, but that was a leading question that went beyond the content that's already in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, indeed. Sorry. I'll not put this question in this context. I'll ask the witness something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said in the same paragraph that the army was disciplined. Which army did you mean?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: If I'm referring to Arkan here, then I meant Arkan and his army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you mean by saying that the troops were disciplined but the people felt uncomfortable?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the troops are concerned, they didn't make any problems. But the people believed that it was a place of worship that should be free of troops, soldiers, and weapons, and if somebody needed to protect it, we, the people, were there to protect it. I had a feeling that he was being somehow supervised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 71. It says: "The troops were very disciplined, but the soldiers who, as part of their training, ran through the village, had an unsettling effect."

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It says again that his troops were disciplined, but every morning as part of their training about 50 of them would run through Dalj and ordinary people would feel intimidated. It seemed to them they were in a kind of barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at paragraph 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In our proofing session, we read this paragraph as well. We compared it with your resignation. First of all, does this paragraph faithfully reflect what you said in your interview with the investigators or has something been left out?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't faithfully reflect what I said because this is about the speaker of the assembly, and this paragraph makes it sound as if it were about the prime minister. One of the reasons for my resignations -- one of the reasons for my resignation were the statements made by the president, et cetera, et cetera. It sounds from this as if it were the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you mean that the word "president" should be followed by "of the assembly"?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that written in your resignation? We will look at it a bit later. But is it clearly written in your letter of resignation?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: My letter of resignation makes it perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If the same questions were put to you today, would you give the same answers as in this statement with the corrections you have just made today and which have been recorded, save for the two paragraphs that you said you couldn't stand by. That's paragraphs 56 and 57.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: With those corrections, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this evidence into -- this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I may have missed it, but I understand there's also a second question required before admission of 92 ter statements about the contents of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Gillett. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that otherwise what is written in your statement is accurate with the corrections just made?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Our Rules require you to say whether the answers you gave in this statement, including the corrections you've made today, are accurate.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the corrections, they are accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, I will start with the last question we discussed; that is, your letter of resignation described in paragraph 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D2 -- no, 1D1264. Tab 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the letter of resignation we discussed?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that on 27 October you submitted your resignation as minister for culture and religion in the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, that it was not given consideration, and you are resubmitting it. I will quote the passage that I'm interested in. You say: "I cite as the most important reasons for my resignation the statements of -- the statements made by members of the government, some members of the government and the president of the assembly without prior consultation with the prime minister and without any stance taken by the assembly or the government on key and decisive issues for the Serbian people in this district and the Serbian Krajina." Was this the passage that you referred to when you said in paragraph 73 that the reasons were not correctly stated?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And it says at the end: "I believe that these and similar acts amount to ignoring the assembly, the government, and the prime minister..." Is this what you meant when you were talking about paragraph 73?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the president of the assembly at that time, the person you referred to in this statement without naming him?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was Ilija Koncarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, since you lived in Dalj, first of all, tell us: How long have you lived in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: From 1955 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Dalj an ethnically mixed community?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What were interethnic relations like, and if they were good, until when?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Interethnic relations were good. There were many ethnically mixed marriages. There had never been any problems. There were Serbs, Croats, Hungarians, some Ruthenians, and there had never been any problems until the HDZ came into power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I ask you to speak a little more slowly. What happened exactly after the HDZ came into power? How did the interethnic relations deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I talk about Dalj because I lived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The question has a leading aspect in saying that the relations deteriorated which hadn't yet come out in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It -- it -- but it refers from his previous answer, that the -- these relations were good until HDZ came to the power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Overruled. Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I repeat the question or you remember it?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No need. I can talk about Dalj and the area surrounding it. Everything was fine even after the local HDZ was established. We, the residents of Dalj, did not have our SDS party. At the time of the elections, we voted for the SDP. But we felt cheated because we had been removed from the constitution as a constituent people and many people started losing their jobs, being dismissed just because they were Serbs. Mistreatment began. Cars were stopped carrying Serbs. The cars were searched. People were searched. Then they started admitting onto the police force people with a problematic past. For instance, in Dalj, an unprecedented thing happened when a man was killed with an axe and the person responsible was just allowed to go scot-free, and he was later admitted into the police, and people understood it as a threat. Another case I can tell you about is when Ivan Andabak returned. He was a Ustasha emigre, and he came to Dalj. By night, people were going about carrying rifles, driving about in a van with open doors. Sometimes haystacks were set on fire. People were brought into the police station, taken into custody. Once I was taken into custody. At the police station in Osijek, I was treated quite well regularly. I can't complain. But bar brawls also became more frequent. I went to see the president of the HDZ to talk to him because I knew the man. We had been to school together. I thought these things would stop. However, assassinations began as well. Somebody shot Zivko Peulic in Osijek. Then another man in Brsadin, then Jovo, Rajkica was killed on his own balcony. We don't know to this day who the shooter was. And Serbs began to join the SDS en masse, although the SDS was not the only party they could join, but people started joining the SDS en masse. And there's another example. At that time I wrote the statute and we held a founding assembly for the Serbian singing society Lira, and the statute was printed in the Cyrillic script, and I went to Osijek to register it. They just sneered at it and refused to register us. So we went on working without the proper license. I did not want to print our programme in the Latin script, although that is something I use when I write something by hand, even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to your last answer, why wouldn't they register your association?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Because the statute was drafted in the Cyrillic script and that the proposed name was the Serbian singing association. They did not want to accept the Cyrillic script although Yugoslavia still existed and both the letters, the Latinic script and the Cyrillic script, were supposed to be equally represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that people started going about with rifles and other long-barreled arms. Who were those people? How did they treat the citizens of Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: They were arrogant. When I say arrogant, I mean they did not ill-treat people but they demonstrated their power. In Erdut they had their own camp. I don't know whether they were HOS members or who they were. I really don't know the name of that group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they cause fear among the Serbs in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, fear, anguish, anger. All of a sudden people started flocking together. I have to tell you that I was stopped by the police several times. My car was searched. The last time that happened I was taken to the Dalj police station from Erdut, and after that I just couldn't take it any longer. I left Dalj about a month and a half before it was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean a month and a half before the 1st of August?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you leave on your own or with your family?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: My whole family. My wife, my daughter, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: To Belgrade to stay with a friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After your departure for Belgrade, did you occasionally return to the territory?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did go to Borovo Selo but never to Dalj before it was liberated. I arrived in Borovo Selo with the barge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were in the area when the incident in Borovo Selo happened on the 2nd of May, 1991. Were you in Dalj at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Dalj on that day. However, since Dalj is not a big place, rumours spread very fast about Borovo having been attacked. We didn't know why. Shooting already started. The distance between Dalj and Savulja is 4 kilometres, and that was where shooting started. I organised 100 people without any arms to go there, to see whether we could stop the shooting in a peaceful manner, to resolve the situation if there was anything to be resolved. We failed in our attempt. We got to the Croatian side but we could not proceed. We were forced to sit down on the asphalt road. That's how the whole thing ended. Later on I heard that some people had gotten killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how that incident in Borovo Selo reflected on the locals of Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. And I learned only later that some people from Dalj did not join me on foot but that -- rather, they got onto boats and they went along the river to Borovo Selo to help. There was war in -- in -- in the offing. Barricades were erected. People started flocking together along the ethnic lines. Serbs communicated only with other Serbs, Croats with other Croats, and there was a visible ethnical division after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After the incident in Borovo Selo, do you know whether that had an impact on the relationship between the people in Dalj and particularly on the attitude of HDZ members towards Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It had already started happening before but all of a sudden things came to a head. Those people became more savage, barricades were erected by Bijelo Brdo, and then a Croatian unit started attacking Bijelo Brdo. I don't know what unit that was. In any case, there were a lot more individual incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the -- what you said about Bijelo Brdo, for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And please slow down.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Very well. After the barricades in Borovo Selo, the other villages also started erecting their own barricades. One of them was at Bijelo Brdo. There was a unit in Erdut, I don't know what unit that was, also attacked Bijelo Brdo. There was shooting. There were people wounded. Many people who worked at Borovo stopped going to work. Also those who worked in Osijek. There were a lot of incidents that just could not be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about that. Why did people stop going to work in Borovo and Osijek?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Fear. Fear was the cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody have any bad experience?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Some people from Dalj did go to Osijek but they ended up being arrested. I remember a man called Sobota who worked at an insurance company and he was arrested in Osijek. People were taken to the police station quite often, and people start fearing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You participated in the battle for Dalj on the 1st of August, 1991. Can you describe your participation in that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I did participate in my own way. We all participated in different ways. On the 31st of July late in the afternoon, I arrived Borovo Selo. However, in the evening people started gathering around the sports hall, and rumours started spreading about people going to liberate Dalj. I was among those people. I was standing there as well. I remember Marko Loncarevic who was also there, and also Sinisa Kazevic [phoen]. They were in the very centre of that group. And also I remember Jovica Vucenovic. They seemed to have been in control, giving orders. There were also some other officers whose names I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say officers were there, were they active-duty officers, reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you who an active officer was and who wasn't because they wore the same uniforms. But I remember a man whose family name was Bencer [phoen]. He was an active-duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that his name was Bencer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a musician and I was opposed to arms. I didn't want to be a hunter. I just don't like arms. Like some people don't like football, I don't like weapons. Marko Loncarevic told me, "Boro, you're going drive a truck." "Very well," said I. I went to fetch the truck that I was assigned. The truck was loaded. I didn't inspect it. There were two trucks. I drove one of them and Mirko Puvaca drove the other. I was assigned a location and the location was Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's specify. When you say Lovas, is that a place or something else?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was just going to say that Lovas is a farm, a cattle farm. It's a farm between Dalj and Savulja, i.e., between Dalj and Borovo Selo. I arrived there. I parked the truck by a canal and I got stuck there. I was looking for something to wedge a wheel and it was only then that I saw weapons, and then I remember that Mirko actually wanted to play a game on me. He knew I didn't like arms, so he gave me a truck full of arms to drive. He -- he was just joking with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you described the whole Dalj action in great detail. I don't want you to repeat any of that. Did you participate in the fighting? Did you use weapons during that action?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I drove a -- a -- the truck. The action was in the direction of Dalj and there was shooting from Dalj. I couldn't go there by truck because the truck was full of weapons. I could not personally participate in the fighting. I could only enter Dalj once it was calm. I was assigned a location. It was the playground in Dalj. I was supposed to bring the truck over there, and somebody was supposed to take it over from me. I wasn't informed who that person would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Milinkovic, we take the first break, 30 minutes. That means that we will be back at 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I tendered the document 1D2328, it was the statement of the witness, I did not mention 2328.1. It was actually a part of this statement. So I would tender this document too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And just to clarify for the record: In Your Honours' decision of 3 September 2014 on this witness, you specified that the Prosecution 65 ter document 2508 would be the photo booklet attached to this witness's statement. I understand it's the same as the 1D2328.1 that my learned friend has just mentioned and on that basis, of course, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D189.187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milinkovic, you were part of the government for a while of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Could you specify the time-period and your post, your position in the government?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact dates. I was nominated to become minister of culture and religion, and I accepted this position. Members of the National Council, when nominated by the assembly onto that government, I accepted the nomination, and that is -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the first headquarters of the government?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: First it was in Dalj in the library, but it was impossible to work there. There were 15 ministries and only one telephone. And the premises were not adequate for the work of the government, so the government moved to Erdut to the building known as Dvorac, the mansion, whereas I stayed in the library in Dalj to be closer to my locals and to keep the library safe from looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember maybe when the government moved to Erdut?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: About 15 days after it was established. Maybe even within ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In what circumstances did the government work?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be more true to say that it didn't work. It didn't have any founding documents. We just had these ministries. We didn't have a grass-root basis. We started from scratch. Everybody had to first form their ministry, beginning with the deputy minister, assistants, staff, et cetera, and only then could we move on to enacting regulations and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government manage to do anything during its short tenure?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it did. I can only speak about my ministry. I didn't have any an insight into the work of other ministries except for the reports regularly submitted at government sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about your ministry? What was done within your field?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all we needed to tour all the museums, all the churches, to assess the damage and to repair it as far as possible, to appoint directors to museums, inspection authorities, and we have managed to done all that. It was quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government have any tools to enforce its decisions? Did it have agencies that would pass on its orders to the local authorities in villages and towns?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I just said. We didn't have local communes. We had Territorial Defence Staffs in many villages over which we didn't have jurisdiction. The army had jurisdiction. Where we had local communes, we collaborated with them. I can give you the example of Dalj. We had a local commune but it was not operative. So the minister himself had to go and visit each place. It was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the army, can you tell us when did the army arrive? From what time did it have a presence in SBWS?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: The army had always been there. Beginning with the 1st of August in Dalj, there was an army presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Radovan Stojicic, Badza, tell you anything; and, if it is familiar, did you have occasion to meet him?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I did have occasion to see Badza but I was never introduced to him. I didn't have much contact with him. I know that he was appointed - although not by us - as commander of the Territorial Defence. I don't know who appointed him. He arrived sometime after the government was established. I met him in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in broad terms, what did these sessions of the SBWS government look like?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: They were very serious, beginning with the security around the building. We always got invitations from the secretary. We always had an agenda. First we would read the record from the previous session, and if there were no objections it would be adopted, and that would be followed by reports from various ministers describing work progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember, did you attend all the sessions?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I always tried to attend. I can't guarantee that I attended every single one, but I tried to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who chaired the sessions?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic. Or sometimes his deputy, Mr. Sabljakovic. Sometimes due to the nature of his work he was away and his deputy prime minister chaired the sessions but it was only rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to you, members of the cabinet, did anyone else come to these sessions of the government?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojicic. There was one colonel, Ristic. Mr. Savo Stupar. I remember once even Mr. Raznjatovic came. Then Mr. Zavisic. And they didn't come all together. One of them would usually would come. I had the impression that they might have been even monitoring our work, keeping an eye on us. They didn't have anything in common. They were neither all from the army or all from the police. There would be even a representative of the Assembly of Vojvodina sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive a salary while you were minister?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never worked for a salary. I only once got coupons for petrol that I collected in order to be able to pay the wages of the people who were working cleaning up the museum in Vukovar. That's the only thing I collected. Otherwise I worked without a salary. And I must say that the money that I received, I got from Mr. Milanovic. I don't know where he got it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said this money went for the cleaning up of the museum in Vukovar, did you mean that it was after the combat in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was after the liberation of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, do you remember in October 1991, was there some kind of mutiny among the members of the Territorial Defence in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember. I remember it because I was at home that night, and somebody came and told me that the men from Dalj had retreated from the line. They don't want to go to the front line. Our stretch was from Trpinja to Borovo. That area had to be liberated. The Trpinja road. And the next day, they mutinied against the army. In fact, against the command. Because every day a stretch of 2 kilometres would be liberated. These people would go back. Some people would get killed. And then the next day they would have to go and liberate the same stretch again. That's why people mutinied. And it was an assembly near the market-place where everything happened. Badza was there and Arkan was there too. Badza probably as the commander of the TO and Arkan as an authority. This is not to detract the authority of Mr. Badza. That's not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said it was a protest against the command, which command?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: You see, my family believed that at that time even they didn't know who was the command. They were under the command of the army, and they protested against the army. They wanted somebody to put some order into how the -- this war was waged instead of go forward and then pull back, because they were commanded by JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just explain what does it mean stop and go, and pull back? I mean, I understand what you mean, but I'd like everybody in the courtroom to understand as well.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: The men were sent every morning to a certain point, and from point A to point B, there were some 5 kilometres that needed to be liberated. So they do it. They go from A to B and liberate it. Then they leave this space empty and go home. And the next day, they do the same job again. But all this time, every day, it costs some lives, and that's why they mutinied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, between that point A, as you said, and point B, there was some fighting involved in order to get to point B?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it is in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And for what reason did these men who reached point B go back?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: They went back because that was the orders given, and that's why they protested against the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the next day they would get orders to go again to fight in order to reach point B, the one they had reached earlier?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So they were thinking that they were making sacrifices for nothing?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, that last question was leading and also was asking the witness to speculate on what other people were thinking, so I'd object to that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What are these people protesting against on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I just told you that the night before I had been in Trpinja. I had travelled there in my own car because I had heard that the men in Dalj had mutinied. It was not my department, but I was just concerned because Dalj was my home town. And then I heard that they mutinied because, as they told me in their own words, they were going to be asked the next day to liberate the same area again, the same stretch.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they talk about the sacrifices they were making, their losses?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: When you have soldiers gathered in one place, always somebody from the back would shout something. I was not there, nor was the government represented there. I don't know anything, save for what I heard from my friends who were there. Many people were shouting the names of their friends who had fallen, and they criticised many people, like Milorad Stricevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at P115, paragraph 111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. It is tab 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we have the text on the screen. You can see who wrote this report, or rather you can see the body who issued it. One part has been redacted. Let us look at the second paragraph where it says that: "On Tuesday 15 October of this year in the morning hours around 300 members of the Dalj TO gathered and at gunpoint forced the members of the Dalj staff and some ministers of the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem to line up before them. A petition on the unbearable living conditions was read. It was said that the situation in Dalj was apocalyptic." Further on there is a reference to the members of the space police. Further on, it is stated that they publicly accused Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, of crimes committed against 40 prisoners. He admitted the guilt, and he said that only the way in which they were executed was in dispute. Could you please tell us whether this report faithfully reflects what happened at the time. If not, what part would you disagree with?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not there. However, I lived there, and I can tell you that it is 100 per cent incorrect that they publicly accused him or brought him out at gunpoint. TO members could not have done that. He came there on his own with Badza. As for some members of the TO Command, I believe that they were all together in it. I don't know what Arkan was saying there. I believe that some inflammatory words were said. And it is not ruled out, it cannot be ruled out, that he did say what it says he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know and the information you have, how come that he found himself there? What is it that he actually said, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: His vocabulary was rather limited. He probably appeared there. Now what he said, I don't know. I wasn't there so I hate to speculate what he might have said. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Don't.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I would rather not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, don't speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go to the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says that the defence commander Badza was given an ultimatum by the fighters to deal with the burning issues within 48 hours. If not, they would take matters into their own hands. They would deal with the people who were tarnishing the reputation of the place and who compounded the situation with their psychotic behaviour. If the ultimatum was not observed, the fighters threatened that they would form a court-martial. Tell me please, according to what you know, did that happen? Did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard anybody mentioning a court-martial, nor was it ever actually established. I don't know if anybody would have dared give an ultimatum to Badza. He had such authority that I don't believe that anybody could have spoken to him in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the commanders of TO units said that they would undertake all the possible measures in order to normalise the situation, and if Raznjatovic or some others who are -- is described here as executors were to oppose them, that they would be done away with?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, it did not happen. It was just a rumour among the fighters. Everybody gave themselves too much importance. This is a report which I wouldn't say is very credible. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you said that the fighters mutinied against the JNA and the -- the orders of false starts and retreats. There's nothing about that in this report. Were there perhaps two different protested in Dalj or was there just this one?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of only that one, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. The question is leading in saying that there is nothing about this in this, report and this is based on the word "mutiny" which originally was inserted into the transcript by the Defence counsel, so we would see this question as a leading question. The word "mutiny" came in earlier in the transcript and was from a question. It wasn't from the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How would you call the event that happened in Dalj? How would you call the rally of about 300 members of the TO and their requests?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: A protest would be a different thing and it involves workers. This was a mutiny of people who didn't want to carry out their tasks. They simple didn't go to the front line on that day. You can call it whatever: A mutiny, a protest. I know what it was all -- all about. I am aware of that case when Arkan and Badza were present at that rally. I don't know of any similar instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you resigned on the 27th of October - we don't have the written text of that resignation - why did you decide to resign as early as that on the 27th of October, only about a month into the functioning of the government?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll give you a few examples. First of all, the government as such did not have any authorities over the TO or the military. We were actually like a local commune -- not even a local commune because a local commune has some powers. For example, we were stopped on various roads by the military. I was stopped on the way to Sodolovci by the army. I told them who I was. But they laughed at my position. Effectively we could not exert our authority over anybody or anything. The only thing that remained for us to do was to deal with social issue, the life of people. If there was a company still operating we could deal with those. That's one of the reason -- reasons. The second reason was that we could not exert any influence on any of the events. We did not have any instruments at -- in place. We did not have any information. We just relied on rumours, on talking to people, so it was impossible to function. That was another reason. I believe that in my resignation I stated that I was not in a position to implement the programme of work in my -- within my purview. That -- those were the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After your second resignation in January 1992, how long did you keep coming to the government meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I kept on attending for a couple of more times after I resigned. And then I turned up once but they had already removed me from my position. I didn't know that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. After the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was set up as well as the regional government of the SBWS, did you have an office in the regional government or in the republican government?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have any positions or functions. I simply set up a cultural centre in Dalj, and I remained working there as the CEO. I stopped being involved in politics. I even funded the cultural centre myself and I paid the workers from my own pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Until 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I moved to Novi Sad, or rather to Beocin. I have to tell you that in 1995 I was in the regional government of Mr. Boro Dzajic [phoen] but that was towards the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milinkovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you'd just give me one minute to set up the podium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milinkovic. My name is Matthew Gillett. We haven't met before. I'm going to ask you some questions on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. If there is anything that is unclear, then please request and I can clarify my question. Firstly, just to check some of the dates. Do I understand correctly that you were living in Dalj until after the Borovo Selo incident in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Then you said earlier today that you left from Dalj to Serbia about a month and a half before the take-over of Dalj on 1st August. So would that be sometime in June that you left to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember when that was. It was just my estimate. I estimated the time because I did not make any notes on which I could rely to give you the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So your recollection of dates from that period is slightly vague; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Then in 1996, you left and moved to Novi Sad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were you living there in 2003 when you gave the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that we've been referring to today?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Beocin in 2003. So you mean Beocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, for the record, which country is that in?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going ask you a question about the Velepromet meeting of 20th November, 1991. You discussed that meeting in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You assume that Arkan travelled with Goran Hadzic to that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I assumed because I saw them together. That doesn't mean that they actually came together. It was just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: My question was whether you made that assumption. And that is correct; right? What was -- sorry, could you say your answer for the record, not just nodding the head?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was my assumption. I assumed that they came together because I saw them together. However, that doesn't necessarily mean that they had arrived together. At that moment, I saw them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: My question is rather concentrated on why you assumed that they travelled together. Now you've said today that it's because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's asked and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, I haven't finished my question yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. -- Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So you said today it was because you saw them together and you meant you saw them together at Velepromet; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw them together. But that does not mean that they had come together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Again, my question is not about whether this was true or not. It's the assumption. Now a Mr. Vojin Susa was also at the Velepromet meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you assume that he came to the Velepromet meeting with Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Miomir Crnogorac was also together with Goran Hadzic at the Velepromet meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you assume that he travelled with Goran Hadzic to the Velepromet meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: It was possible, yes. But I never gave it a second thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you think now that Miomir Crnogorac travelled with Goran Hadzic to the Velepromet meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't think anything. He could have arrived on his own. I don't know. I'm not concerned. I don't think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What was it about the relationship between Hadzic and Arkan that made you assume that they travelled to the meeting together?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, my question this time was focused on the relationship between these two, and there is a basis in the statement for asking this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Shall I repeat my question, or did you catch it?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the question. My assumption was based on the fact that they were standing together. A thought crossed my mind: They probably arrived together. There was no any other special reason why they should have been together, because I never saw Mr. Arkan as Mr. Hadzic's escort, ever before that. That was the first time I ever saw them together in a meeting or in a rally or anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You assumed that they travelled together because they had a good relationship together. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had a good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And it's because they both travelled to the Velepromet meeting from Erdut -- I'll repeat my question. You assumed this also because they both travelled to the Velepromet meeting from Erdut; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they arrived together from Erdut. I don't know that. I don't know. I simply can't say because Mr. Arkan could have been in Vukovar as well. I know that he had participated in the liberation of Vukovar. I don't know. I can't claim that they arrived together. It was just my assumption. It -- it was my way of thinking at the time. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Milinkovic, you were a member of the Defence Staff in Dalj in August 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I was never a member of a staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know who the members of the Dalj Defence Staff were in August 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know all of them. I could perhaps remember two or three people. Pavle Milovanovic, Djuras Marjanac [as interpreted], and Ilija Mutevic [phoen]. I'm not even sure of his first name. I suppose it's Ilija.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could it be Ilija Utovic?

utterances.speaker: BORIVOJE MILINKOVIC
